messages.subject: Re: draw sem model
messages.subject_clean: draw sem model
messages.body_plain:
These aren't lavaan questions, but perhaps I can point you in the right direction.

> 1. is this the best way or there is another better way to draw?

If you want more control over exactly how you want your diagram to look, there are guides (#18 and #26) for how to create path diagrams manually in Word and in Dia (an open-source alternative to Adobe Illustrator and Microsoft Visio):

http://crmda.ku.edu/kuant-guides

> 2. how to put the estimators values on the arrows in diagram?

The help page tells you what labels are available, using the second argument "what":

?semPlot::semPaths

For example, you can insert raw coefficients using

semPaths(fit, "est", title = FALSE, curvePivot = TRUE)

or standardized coefficients using

semPaths(fit, "std", title = FALSE, curvePivot = TRUE)

Terry

messages.subject_clean: interpretation of sem results when data are binary
messages.body_plain:
On 05/01/2014 03:56 PM, vasilis nikolaou wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> Does anyone know how to interpret the results  of a SEM when all
> variables are binary? I used the link="logit" when fitting the model.

The 'link' argument is just a placeholder, and will only be used when
estimator is MML (marginal ML). It is ignored for all other estimator.

By default, lavaan uses the WLSMV estimator, and here we use the
"probit" link.

You will need to find yourself a good book and/or tutorial to help you
with the interpretation of probits and thresholds.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Different measurement invariance results from lavaan and Mplus7
messages.body_plain:
On 04/26/2014 07:28 AM, Amin Mousavi wrote:
> Hi Yves,
>
> Following my previous question and our discussion, I ran a simple
> multigroup CFA using Mplus and lavaan.The data and Mplus output are
> attached.I used this codes for lavaan:
>
> model<-'com=~q1+q2+q3+q4+q5+q6+q7+q8+q9'
>
> m<-cfa(model,data=data,group="age",ordered=c("q1","q2","q3","q4","q5","q6","q7","q8","q9"),group.equal=c("loadings","thresholds"))
>

> I used *group.equal=c("loadings","thresholds")* because Mplus by default

> assumes that factor loadings and thresholds are equal across groups in
> multigroup CFA.

But your (restricted) Mplus model (see DIFFTEST.out) is a totally
different model. In your Mplus syntax, you have constrained the
thresholds, factor means, and scale factors to be equal across groups.
But NOT the loadings.

> using *lavTestLRT()* I got this:

>
> Scaled Chi Square Difference Test (test = scaled.shifted)
>
>       Df AIC BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
> fa  108         1448.3
> fa1 153         1557.5     48.692      45     0.3268
>

> *lavTestLRT()* is reporting normal theory chi-squares (i.e. 1448.3 &

> 1557) and not the scaled ones.

The chi-squares or not normal theory based. But they are unscaled. That
is because we 'scale' the difference between the two unscaled chi-square
values in a scale chi-square difference test. See the Satorra (&
Bentler) papers describing these tests.

Yves.

messages.subject: Fixing correlation between latent variables to 1
messages.subject_clean: Fixing correlation between latent variables to 1
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I'm relatively new with structural modeling, and especially with lavaan and R. Is there a way to fix a correlation between exogenous latent variables to 1? I am aware I could just define a new factor encompassing the previous ones, but I would like to explore the issue of equivalent models this way. I have tried defining it with the help of equal() and the relation of correlation and covariance:
emp <- 'af =~ 1*E01+E03+E05+E09+E11+E13+E15+E17+E19+E21
cf =~ 1*E02+E04+E06+E08+E10+E14+E16+E18+E20+E22
rc =~ 1*E03+E04+E11+E18+E20+E22
af~~1*sqrt(equal("af~~af")*equal("cf~~cf"))*cf
cf~~1*sqrt(equal("rc~~rc")*equal("cf~~cf"))*rc'

But this only resulted in covariance between af~~cf and cf~~rc being equal. I have not found another way to do it, could you please advise me why does this not function and/or suggest another way to accomplish this?

Thank you very much,

Una

messages.subject: Re: Fixing correlation between latent variables to 1
messages.subject_clean: Fixing correlation between latent variables to 1
messages.body_plain:
A correlation implies that the two variables are standardized.  That standardization will generally be inconsistent with scaling the factors by fixing a loading to 1.  But you can standardize the factors in several ways, including:

NA the first loading on each factor, then
Fix the variance of each factor to 1, then
Fix the covariance between factors to 1

Ed Rigdon

Apologises, I press the wrong key. Another possibly is that the first item for Planning_Organising construct has such low factor loading that it is not considered as being related to the model, leading to model under identification.

I am relatively new to SEM and I am trying to make sure that my steps in the analysis aren't wrong.

Thank you so much for helping!
Kind regards,
Aiden

messages.body_plain:
Aiden--
     I'm sorry to be negative here, but yes, the third and fourth factors especially will not be well-defined and stable, because there are few indicators and the indicators are weak.  This may well explain the factor correlation so close to 1.0.  Of course the chi-square value is poor, with n > 7,000, but CFI is also quite poor, suggesting--as the weak Loadings also suggest--that the indicators do not strongly covary.  In other words, there is not that much covariance to explain.
     The negative thresholds are not an issue--those are like standard normal cut points, so a 0 value means that the threshold falls halfway through the data, and negative values just mean that less than half the data falls to the left of the threshold.  You could generate frequencies for your observed variables and see that the threshold values make sense.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject: coding question - higher order predictors
messages.subject_clean: coding question - higher order predictors
messages.body_plain:
Hello:

I have a question about how to code a particular type of higher order interaction. Basically, I have latent variables that represent behavioral classes (e.g. aggression, courtship) which have specific predictors (scores based on specific behaviors). So the model structure (simplified) is something like this:

aggression =~ x1 + x2 + x3
courtship =~ x4 + x5 + x6 + x7
escape =~ x8 +x9 +x10

I can get this to run and it looks pretty good. What I would like to do now is ask whether hormones influence the latent behavioral classes. So for example, do testosterone levels predict all latent variable or only aggression and courtship? I'm not sure how to do this because the hormones levels are something that I measured, not a higher order latent variable (i.e. I want to ask if the effect is causal). I've know I can just include the hormones as another set of predictors for multiple latent variable, but I'm not sure this is the appropriate strategy.

Any help on how to code this properly is great appreciated!
eva

messages.subject: Re: "number of observations"
messages.subject_clean: "number of observations"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

My guess is that this is related to missing data. By default lavaan uses listwise deletion.If the number of observations used and total reported in the output differ, it is likely because of listwise deletion. To use other methods of missing data handling you can use the "missing = " argument to the cfa/sem/lavaan functions (for FIML) or the runMI function in semTools  (for multiple imputation).

Hope this helps,

Alex

On 05/04/2014 04:12 PM, Aiden Loe wrote:
> Hi Yves,
>
> Could I just check with you, a warning message suggest that the latent
> variables are not positive definite. After inspecting, it all seems to
> be positive.

Perhaps I should clarify the meaning of positive definite. A symmetric
matrix is positive definite if all its eigenvalues are (strictly) larger
than zero. So you can test this with:

eigen( inspect(modelcfa3.1, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") )$values

If the negative value is really, really tiny, it is probably safe, and
you can ignore the warning.

But judging from your factor correlations, it looks like the two latent
variables 'Analytical_Thinking' and 'Planning_Organising' (corr = 0.978)
are almost identical. I would remove one of the two, or rethink the
measurement model (ie the indicators) for these two latent variables.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Fixing correlation between latent variables to 1
messages.body_plain:
On 05/04/2014 10:47 PM, Una wrote:
> Hello!
>
> I'm relatively new with structural modeling, and especially with lavaan
> and R. Is there a way to fix a correlation between exogenous latent
> variables to 1? I am aware I could just define a new factor encompassing
> the previous ones, but I would like to explore the issue of equivalent
> models this way. I have tried defining it with the help of equal() and
> the relation of correlation and covariance:
> emp <- 'af =~ 1*E01+E03+E05+E09+E11+E13+E15+E17+E19+E21
> cf =~ 1*E02+E04+E06+E08+E10+E14+E16+E18+E20+E22
> rc =~ 1*E03+E04+E11+E18+E20+E22
> af~~1*sqrt(equal("af~~af")*equal("cf~~cf"))*cf
> cf~~1*sqrt(equal("rc~~rc")*equal("cf~~cf"))*rc'

Try this:

af =~ NA*E01+E03+E05+E09+E11+E13+E15+E17+E19+E21
cf =~ NA*E02+E04+E06+E08+E10+E14+E16+E18+E20+E22
rc =~ NA*E03+E04+E11+E18+E20+E22

# standardized latent variables
af ~~ 1*af
cf ~~ 1*cf
rc ~~ 1*rc

# force unit correlations
af ~~ 1*cf
af ~~ 1*rc
cf ~~ 1*rc

The fit of this model should be identical to a model where you have only
a single factor.

Yves

>                        ug ~ 0*smi + 0*sex
>                        fdb ~ ug + 0*smi + 0*sex'
>
> path.model.version2 <- 'ww ~ ug
>                        smi ~ sex
>                        fdb ~ ug'

The second one only uses a subset of the variables. You can not compare
version 1 vs version 2. From what you describe, you need version 1: all
the variables, but some paths fixed to zero.

> 2. During the model simplification process, do I have to compare somehow
> the differently structured models? (e.g. Chi-sqr test, or Anova, etc.)

It seems you are using path analysis in an exploratory fashion. Usually,
we use a confirmatory approach, and we only test those models that we
have pre-specified.

Note that all model respecifications may work for your particular sample
only. That is, the changes may not generalize to new samples.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Means comparison in Lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Means comparison in Lavaan
messages.body_plain:
On 04/23/2014 04:32 PM, Anna Jakovleva wrote:
> Is there any possibility in lavaan to compute mean differences of groups
> on a latent variable and their significance (comparable to the anova
> function in R)?

Well, first you need to establish measurement invariance. But suppose
you have measurement invariance, you need to constrain the factor
loadings AND intercepts to be equal (I am assuming all indicators are
continuous), by using group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts").

Then, by default, the factor means of the first group will be fixed to
zero (=reference group), but the other factor means are estimated, and
can be interpreted as the difference between those groups and the
reference groups. And you get a significance test.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
To add to Yves, don't specify so much in your initial model. All those parameters will a) make identification difficult if not impossible, and b) make interpreting the model difficult if not impossible. Start with a very basic hypothesis and move up from there, comparing not only parameters in the equations but also overall model fit.

A couple things that you need to do after you run that first model that converges. Look at the ft indices- how far off is RMSEA from .05, how far from 1 are the CFI etc? That initial chi2 test is mostly useless in my experience (others may have differing opinions). Also run the modification indices to seen where your model can be statistically improved (using theory to decide what changes to make). My bet is you will see that big factor with tons of indicators broken out into smaller factors.

One last thing I noticed you have a very high correlation between two factors. Wen you do the mod indices you will see a ton there and it gets confusing. As a starting point I would focus on the changes related to the indicators in the factors that are so highly correlated. As it stands my bet is you woul have low discriminant validity between those factors.

messages.body_plain:
On 05/08/2014 04:19 PM, Edward Rigdon wrote:
> In the early 1990s, Bekker, Merckens and Wansbeek developed Turbo
> Pascal routines implementing an augmented Jacobian approach to
> evaluating identification.

I have no access to the book (which is out of print), but it should be
relatively straightforward to do this using lavaan (although is not
always clear how the 'Jacobian' is defined).

But for a simple model, you could do something along the lines of:

library(lavaan)
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)

# get 'Jacobian' using an internal function
# do not try this at home (the name of the function will change soon)
JAC <- lavaan:::computeDelta(lavmodel=fit@Model)[[1]]

# full rank? ncol(JAC) == 21
qr(JAC)$rank # also 21

So this is an identified model. What happens if we have an
under-identified model:

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
               speed   =~ NA*x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)

# get 'Jacobian'
JAC <- lavaan:::computeDelta(lavmodel=fit@Model)[[1]]

# full rank? ncol(JAC) == 22
qr(JAC)$rank # 21 (<22)

The rank is 21, while we have 22 free parameters, suggesting that the
model is not identified.

I will investigate this further and perhaps provide a public function
for testing this in the near future.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: how to "switch off" the covariance between two exogenous variables (not latent variables) in lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: how to "switch off" the covariance between two exogenous variables (not latent variables) in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
On 05/11/2014 10:30 AM, Bin Chen wrote:
> Hi all,
> I am a bit confused about how to tell lavaan "don't include the
> covariance between two exogenous variables"

> Because the two exogenous variables were manipulated by me, they should
> not, and they cannot have any correlation...

By default, lavaan uses fixed.x = TRUE, which implies that lavaan will
NOT model/estimate the variances and covariances of the exogenous
variables in the model. The variances/covariances will simply be fixed
at their sample values. If the sample covariance happens to be zero, so
be it.

> I tried fixed.x = T or F, they give me the same results. the degree of
> freedom didn't change.

They shouldn't change, unless you restrict some variances/covariances.

> It seems a very simple model C ~ A + B cannot be tested in lavaan.

mod <- 'C ~ A + B' with fixed.x = TRUE is what you should do (and this
is the default). This is exactly as in regression. Do you 'force' a
correlation between predictors to be zero in a regression context?
Usually not. You just leave them as there are, and this is the default
behaviour of fixed.x = TRUE.

If you *really* must force a covariance to be zero, then you should:

1) use fixed.x = FALSE (since you will model them)
2) add 'A ~~ 0*B' to the model syntax.

Yves.

messages.subject: is simsem not applying the Satorra-Bentler correction right?
messages.subject_clean: is simsem not applying the Satorra-Bentler correction right?
messages.body_plain:
hello everyone. either i am doing something wrong or simsem is not correctly implementing the Satorra-Bentler correction to the chi-square test of model fit.

i'm re-doing some of the simulations in:

Curran, P. J., West, S. G., & Finch, J. F. (1996). The robustness of test statistics to nonnormality and specification error in confirmatory factor analysis. Psychological methods, 1(1), 16.

they're relatively straightforward, using sample sizes of N = 100, 200, 500 and 1000 and non-normality conditions of skewness/kurtosis of 2/7 and 3/21.

i am looking at calculating the empirical rejection rates from the Satorra-Bentler chi-square, but simsem's proportion of rejected models are simply too high. and it doesn't matter how large the sample size is, they always remain at ~20% (when we know they should get closer and closer to the nominal 5%, particularly after sample size gets large).

the only thing i'm changing from what Curran et.al <http://et.al>. did is that they did 500 replications and i'm doing 1000. so, all in all, either i'm not calculating the rejection rates correctly or simsem is not correctly implementing the Satorra-Bentler correction.

if the data is normally-distributed, nothing happens and everything works the way it's supposed to.

library(simsem)

mod1 <- '   nu1 =~ 0.7*y1 +0.7*y2 +0.7*y3
            nu2 =~ 0.7*y4 +0.7*y5 +0.7*y6
            nu3 =~ 0.7*y7 +0.7*y8 +0.7*y9

            nu1 ~~ 0.3*nu3
    nu1 ~~ 0.3*nu2
            nu2 ~~ 0.3*nu3

            nu1 ~~ 1*nu1
            nu2 ~~ 1*nu2
            nu3 ~~ 1*nu3

y1 ~~ 0.51*y1
y2 ~~ 0.51*y2
y3 ~~ 0.51*y3
y4 ~~ 0.51*y4
y5 ~~ 0.51*y5
y6 ~~ 0.51*y6
y7 ~~ 0.51*y7
y8 ~~ 0.51*y8
y9 ~~ 0.51*y9
'

run1 <- '   nu1 =~ NA*y1 + y2 + y3
            nu2 =~ NA*y4 + y5 + y6
            nu3 =~ NA*y7 + y8 + y9

            nu1 ~~ nu3
    nu1 ~~ nu2
            nu2 ~~ nu3

            nu1 ~~ 1*nu1
            nu2 ~~ 1*nu2
            nu3 ~~ 1*nu3
'

dist <- bindDist(skewness=c(rep(2,9)), kurtosis=c(rep(7,9)))

Output <- sim(1000, n=500, run1, indDist=dist, generate=mod1, estimator="ml", lavaanfun="cfa", test="Satorra-Bentler")

sum(Output@fit$pvalue<.05)/1000
[1] 0.217

> Hello, I am trying to simulate a simple path model with lavaan, using

>

>

True. This is a bug in 0.5-16. It happens if you specify thresholds in
the syntax, and you have exogenous covariates.

The best approach here is indeed to simulate the data as if everything
is continuous, and in a second step discretize the categorical variable
using the threshold(s).

Yves.

messages.subject: CFA with ordinal indicators: cfa() vs. lavaan()
messages.subject_clean: CFA with ordinal indicators: cfa() vs. lavaan()
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to fit a multi-group CFA model with ordinal indicators. I would like to know if I got all lavaan specifications right for this kind of model. Therefore, I first tried my hand on the HS data. I fitted the basic multi-group model (ML estimator), then the multi-group CFA model with ordinal indicators, and then the multi-group LAVAAN model with ordinal indicators. When I fit the last two models (cfa and lavaan for ordinal indicators), I get exactly the same output (df, statistics, indexes, number of estimated/non-estimated parameters, values of the parameters, etc.). However, as a lavaan newbie, I do not want to take any chances and thus thought it would be wise to get confirmation (especially about potential redundancies in the syntax). Here are the syntaxes:

MULTI-GROUP MODEL (ML)
HS.model <-
'visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed =~ x7 + x8 + x9'
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, group = "school")

MULTIGROUP-MODEL (WLSMV) - CFA
#create 4 categories for each continuous variable
DF=HolzingerSwineford1939 #copy data frame into new object
#recode in categorical variables
vec=c("x1","x2","x3","x4","x5","x6","x7","x8","x9")#vector of variables names
MinusSD=function(x){mean(x)-sd(x)}#functions to simplify recoding
PlusSD=function(x){mean(x)+sd(x)}
#create 4 categories
library(car)
for (i in vec)
  { DF[,i]=recode(DF[,i],"lo:MinusSD(DF[,i])=0;MinusSD(DF[,i]):mean(DF[,i])=1;
                           mean(DF[,i]):PlusSD(DF[,i])=2;PlusSD(DF[,i]):hi=3")}
for (i in vec) {DF[,i]<-ordered(DF[,i])}#order
table(DF$x1);class(DF$x1)

HS.model <-
'visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed =~ x7 + x8 + x9'
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = DF, group = "school",estimator="WLSMV")
summary(fit)
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = DF, group = "school",estimator="WLSMV",group.equal="thresholds")

MULTIGROUP-MODEL (WLSMV) - LAVAAN
HS.model <-
'visual =~ 1*x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ 1*x4 + x5 + x6
speed =~ 1*x7 + x8 + x9
#cov.lv <http://cov.lv>.
visual ~~ textual
visual ~~ speed
textual ~~ speed
#var.lv <http://var.lv>.
visual ~~ visual
speed ~~ speed
textual ~~ textual
#scales y
x1 ~*~ x1
x2 ~*~ x2
x3 ~*~ x3
x4 ~*~ x4
x5 ~*~ x5
x6 ~*~ x6
x7 ~*~ x7
x8 ~*~ x8
x9 ~*~ x9'
fit <- lavaan(HS.model,auto.th <http://auto.th>=TRUE,data=DF,group="school",estimator="WLSMV",group.equal="thresholds")

Thanks in advance,

Jeffrey Henry

Dear all,

I would like to fit a model with nine variables (no latent), including three endogenous and six exogenous.

One of the endogenous variables is a categorical (DAISIE.estab.DCH) coded as a binary (1/0). Therefore I use the WLSMV estimator.

Regarding the exogenous variables: EGF.perherb and EGF.annherb are two dummies used to code a three-level categorical variable; GRIN.Eur and EGF.veg are also binary variables (yes/no coded as 1/0).

Without any constraint (model1 below), the model is not identified (0 degrees of freedom, too many free parameters to be estimated compared to the number of variables). Now, when I fix the variances of all exogenous and endogenous variables to 1 (model2 below), the model is identified. However, rather than fixing variances and covariances I wanted to specify meanstructure=false, so that the model does not estimate the intercepts of the variables. But this is obviously not compatible with the WLSMV estimator, since it is a "mean and variance-adjusted" WLS method.

The fit of the model is bad anyway, but this is another matter. Here, I would like to ask whether what I do is correct (which I suspect not). Then, my questions are:

1) Do I properly handle the categorical variables (endogenous and exogenous)? If not, what am I doing wrong or what am I missing here?
2) Do I need to use the ordered=c("...") argument to specify which variables are binary or ordinal, or is specifying WLSMV as an estimator sufficient (given that these variables are already specified as factors in my data frame)?
3) Is there no estimator other than WLSMV that I can use here? In other words, do I necessarily need to estimate the intercepts of the variables in this model?
4) Given that the WLSMV requires means and variances, what is going on when I fix variances to 1?
5) The use of WLSMV implies a "scaled.shifted" test, right? It would be unsuitable here to use another test? (e.g. the Bollen-Stine bootstrap approach)

Noëlie

messages.subject: Re: negative variance
messages.subject_clean: negative variance
messages.body_plain:
The two warnings are (almost certainly) about the same thing.  A residual variance is the part of the variance of a dependent variables that is not "explained" or accounted for by the predictors--equal to (1 – R2) times the total variance of the dependent variable.  Variances are supposed to be positive, and the same goes for variance components.  But your model gives rise to a residual variance that is negative.  This can happen due to random sampling error--where a very small true value will sometimes produce a negative estimate--but it can also be a sign of a problem in your model.
--Ed Rigdon

Sent from my iPad

messages.subject: Re: SEM Estimates for measurement model
messages.subject_clean: SEM Estimates for measurement model
messages.body_plain:
This is not necessarily a problem. It's possible to have regression coefficients greater than 1 even in a regression model, but it's a possible sign that you have a collinearity problem, or that you have a misspecified model.

Here's an example:

library(QuantPsyc)
set.seed(123)
x <- rnorm(10)
y <- rnorm(10) + x^2 + x^3
x2 <- x^2
x3 <- x^3
x4 <- x^4
lm.beta(lm(y ~ x + x2 + x3 ))
.
And here's a short paper that explains how it happens:
http://www.ssicentral.com/lisrel/techdocs/HowLargeCanaStandardizedCoefficientbe.pdf

Was the same estimator used? Do things like the sample size, chi-square and df match?

(If you can send something which allows people to run it easily, that's easier for use to try it, and which contains your complete code so that we can run exactly what you ran, for example we don't know what item.list contains. )

Here's a small example, which gives me the same results from Lavaan and Mplus.

R code:
setwd("c:/temp")
library(lavaan)
set.seed(12345)

df <- as.data.frame(matrix(rbinom(prob=0.4, size=1, 2000), ncol=4))
df.n <- df
names(df.n) <- c("q1", "q2", "q3", "q4")

mod2Fit <- "s =~ q1 + q2 + q3 + q4"

cong.fit <- cfa(mod2Fit, data=df.n, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,
           mimic="Mplus", parameterization="delta", ordered=names(df.n))
summary(cong.fit)
write.table(df, "test.dat", row.names=FALSE, col.names=FALSE)

Mplus code:

DATA: FILE = c:\temp\test.dat;
VARIABLE:  NAMES ARE q1-q4;
CATEGORICAL ARE q1-q4;
MODEL:
Skill by q1* q2-q4 ;
Skill@1;

Jeremy

lavaan reports it uses DWLS.  MPlus reports it uses WLSMV.  As near as I can tell from the documentation, these estimators are the same.

Both software packages report having read all 500 records from the data file.

MPlus output cautions that the Chi-square value is not to be trusted with the WLSMV estimator.  So I'm loathe to put much weight by a comparison of that particular item.  The degrees of freedom are the same, though.

I have also tried different starting conditions and convergence criteria; these seem not to change the estimates any.

I originally omitted the code for item.list and itlist because they are generated based on the number of columns in the data set (I am running many other cases), and I thought it would be a distraction.  I have added that code back in to my summary document, though.

Please find attached an updated summary of code and results, lavaan_vs_MPlus_2.pdf.  For convenience, I have re-attached the data set test_data_lavaan_vs_mplus.txt.

Thank you again for your assistance.

Dear Colleagues,

I'd like the help of someone with expertise in the use of Lavaan.

The issue is that by passing from Amos to Lavaan, I have had a problem with the number of DF reported in the model.

I have estimated a model with AMOS (with 16 DF) (please see attached)

I have then been asked to check the re-run the model with the satorra-bentler scaled chi-square with robust standard errors. Because Amos does not support this feature, I have run the model in Lavaan with the following code. I have now obtained virtually the same results (in terms of regression weights) but only 13 DF

C.model<-'
MHSc ~ RIDSc
CM ~ MHSc
CEVAL ~ MHSc
PInteraction ~ MHSc
PInteraction ~ PQuantCont
Pr ~ CM
Pr ~ CEVAL
Pr ~ PInteraction
Pr ~ PD

CEVAL ~~ PInteraction
CEVAL ~~ CM
PInteraction ~~ CM
'
fit <- sem(C.model, data = c, estimator = "MLM")
summary(fit, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit)

I am not an expert in the use of R and even less of the lavaan package. There must be something I am overlooking here. Any suggestion that could point me toward the right direction would be very much appreciated.

Thank you very much for your time,

John

it's a bit unusual that you don't want to have these paths - it's like a multiple regression, you allow your predictors to correlate, and the multiple regression doesn't make sense if you don't.

But if you really don't want them, fixed.x=FALSE will do it. As in:

fit <- sem(C.model, data = c, estimator = "MLM", fixed.x=FALSE)

Jeremy

On 05/15/2014 07:12 PM, Jeremy Miles wrote:
>

The difference between fixed.x=TRUE and fixed.x=FALSE is that the latter
estimates the variances/covariances of the exogenous variables, while
the former simply takes the sample values.

But in both settings, the variances/covariances are always included by
default (if using the sem() or cfa() functions). Forcing the covariances
among exogenous variables to be zero seems strange to me. This may
perhaps make sense in an experimental design, but not for observational
studies.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: categorical endogenous variable and WLSMV estimator
messages.subject_clean: categorical endogenous variable and WLSMV estimator
messages.body_plain:
On 05/12/2014 06:08 PM, Noëlie Maurel wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> I would like to fit a model with nine variables (no latent), including
> three endogenous and six exogenous.
>
> One of the endogenous variables is a categorical (DAISIE.estab.DCH)
> coded as a binary (1/0). Therefore I use the WLSMV estimator.
>
> Regarding the exogenous variables: EGF.perherb and EGF.annherb are two
> dummies used to code a three-level categorical variable; GRIN.Eur and
> EGF.veg are also binary variables (yes/no coded as 1/0).

So far, so good.

> Without any constraint (model1 below), the model is not identified (0
> degrees of freedom

Hold on. If you have df=0, your model is just identified. You just have
a saturated model. There is nothing wrong with that. But you do not get
a goodness-of-fit test.

BUT, you should not use std.ov=TRUE. You don not want to 'standardize'
the dummy variables. If you must standardize variables, do this in your
data.frame before calling lavaan.

Also, have you declared the endogenous categorical as 'ordered' in your
data.frame? I don't think so, since I do not see any thresholds in your
output. You can also use the ordered= argument in the sem() function.
Please see:

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

> However, rather than fixing variances and covariances I wanted to
> specify meanstructure=false

Nope. You need the thresholds.

> Then, my questions are:
>
> 1) Do I properly handle the categorical variables (endogenous and
> exogenous)?

No. See above. You need the ordered= argument.

> 2) Do I need to use the ordered=c("...") argument to specify which
> variables are binary or ordinal

Yes.

> 3) Is there no estimator other than WLSMV that I can use here?

Perhaps ULSMV, but that will not solve your problem.

> 4) Given that the WLSMV requires means and variances

WLSMV does not require means and variances. The 'MV' only refers to the
correction of the test statistic. It is (or was) a 'mean and variance
adjusted' correction.

> 5) The use of WLSMV implies a "scaled.shifted" test, right? It would be
> unsuitable here to use another test? (e.g. the Bollen-Stine bootstrap
> approach)

You can use estimator="DWLS", in combination with se="bootstrap" and
test="bootstrap". This will take a while, but it should work.

Yves.

On 05/12/2014 04:50 PM, Dr. Hans Hansen wrote:
> however, when i look at the first and second post, than dropping one
> variable doesn't result in a nested model, and i cannot test this way,
> right?

I'm not entirely sure what you are looking for, but if you want to
'remove' a variable from a model, without actually removing it from the
set of variables, then you can use something like this:

# 'remove variable x9'

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
               speed   =~ x7 + x8

               x9 ~~ x9
               x9 ~~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8
             '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
fit

This should give the same fit (and warnings) as

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6

               speed   =~ x7 + x8 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
fit

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: CFA with ordinal indicators: cfa() vs. lavaan()
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the great support! I was asking this question because I am running into an odd problem with my own data. I am testing a general-specific (or bifactor) model with one general factor + 3 specific factors,  on a twin sample (grouping=MZ,DZ). Each item is assessed twice, for each twin (twin 1, twin 2) and is rated on a 4-point scale. When I treat the data as continuous (MLR), the model runs smoothly and provides results coherent with the literature and what is expected from twin models. However, when I treat the data as ordinal (estimator="WLSMV"), inter-factor covariances (i.e., twin1-twin2 covariance for each factor) are > 1. This is unexpected as I set the mean to 0 and variance to 1 for these factors so that, to my understanding, they should behave as correlations (which they do in the MLR model and other models I have tested). Also, the estimates are superior to one and the std.all are equal to the estimates. I was not sure whether there was a problem with my own data or the way I specified the bifactor model. Therefore, I took to the HS data again to sort it out. Successively, I
1) considered (x1-x9) as the variables for twin 1 , and created a second set of variables for twin 2 by adding random noise (x1b-x9b);
2) recoded all observed variables as categorical, and;
3) tested the bifactor model with all relevant specifications for interchangeable dyads (i.e., equal loadings, thresholds and scaling according to school group (taken as an equivalent for MZ:DZ), but also to member of each dyad (twin 1 - twin 2)) - see attached syntax. Note that the structure of correlations in the two school groups is not like MZ:DZ (where correlations twin1 twin 2 in MZ > DZ). But because here I fit only the phenotypic CFA without the genetic structure, I think that is ok for the example. I also obtain inter-factor covariance > 1 in the HS data. Is there something wrong with the specifications (see below)? Or, is it sth normal in threshold models? Or identification issue or estimation problem?

Thanks in advance,

Jeffrey Henry

> > any chances and thus thought it would be wise to get confirmation

> looking at the parameter table:
>
> parTable(fit)
>
> If two parameter tables are identical, the models are identical.
>
> Yves.

It appears you are passing a list to the function rather than a data.frame (which lavaan requires). Use something like as.data.frame() on your data object to change the object class. It's also possible that the model is not uniquely identified since the third latent variable only has 2 indicators (3 are generally required, but two are possible with additional constraints).

However, it could be something else entirely, but if further issues arise I don't think I'll be able to detect it from syntax alone (you're welcome to send your dataset to my email if you'd prefer not to post it publicly). Cheers

Phil

Dear All,
I am fitting a simple univariate ACE model (A=genetic, C=shared environment, E=non-shared environment) in a twin sample.
I want to regress out sex and age not before, but inside the model. However, because sex for twin 1 and sex for twin 2 are the same in identical twins, the correlated 1. So I get a warning.
Warning message:
In lav_samplestats_from_data(lavdata = lavdata, missing = lavoptions$missing,  :
  lavaan WARNING sample covariance can not be inverted in group: 2
I don't think it is a problem as the model runs fine and the estimates make sense. But I wanted to check with you.
 Also, my end aim is to regress age and sex on latent factors in a CFA. However, in a CFA, the latent factor is standardized (mean =0, and variance =1) for scaling (to be fair, i'm not sure that the mean = 0 is necessary). In this case, I wonder if regressing make sense: how to regress out the effect of predictors on the mean when the mean is fixed to 0?

Below is the simulated data set for the univariate analysis, with correlation .50 between twin1 and t2 in Dizygotic Twins and correlation .70 in identical twins, indicating moderate heritability. I also included an age variable that correlate .20 and is the same for twin 1 and 2 (born the same day). Sex is the same in MZ and diff in DZ. It does not correlate with the dependent variable because I was not sure how to simulate that, but I don't think it matters for the example.
Thanks a lot!!!

#Create a data frame
seed(12345)
n=1000
#DZ data
DZt1=rnorm(n)
DZt2=0.4*DZt1+sqrt(1-0.4)*rnorm(n)
cor(DZt1,DZt2)
AgeDZ=.2*DZt1 + .2*DZt2 + rnorm(n,0,sqrt(1 - (.2*.2)^2))
cor(cbind(DZt1,DZt2,AgeDZ))
DZ1sex=sample(c(0,1),1000,replace=T)
DZ2sex=sample(c(0,1),1000,replace=T)
#MZ data
MZt1=rnorm(n)
MZt2=0.7*MZt1+sqrt(1-0.7)*rnorm(n)
AgeMZ=.2*MZt1 + .2*MZt2 + rnorm(n,0,sqrt(1 - (.2*.2)^2))
cor(cbind(MZt1,MZt2,AgeMZ))
MZ1sex=MZ2sex=sample(c(0,1),1000,replace=T)
#final data frame
DF=data.frame(X1=c(DZt1,MZt1),X2=c(DZt2,MZt2),sex1=c(DZ1sex,MZ1sex),sex2=c(DZ2sex,MZ2sex),age=c(AgeDZ,AgeMZ),zygos=factor(c(rep("DZ",1000),rep("MZ",1000))))
#correlation structure
Vec=c("X1","X2","sex1","sex2","age")
round(cor(DF[DF$zygos=="MZ",Vec]),2)#correlation between sex1 and sex2 is 1 in monozygotic twins
round(cor(DF[DF$zygos=="DZ",Vec]),2)

#fit univariate model regressed on Age + sex
UnivACE <-
  '
#factor loadings
a1=~c(la,la)*X1#loadings are equal in the two groups (same label = la)
a2=~c(la,la)*X2#and in the twin one and two(same label = la)
c1=~c(lc,lc)*X1
c2=~c(lc,lc)*X2
e1=~c(le,le)*X1
e2=~c(le,le)*X2
#covariances
a1~~c(0.5,1)*a2
c1~~1*c2
#fix variances and means for observed and factors
X1~~0*X1
X2~~0*X2#
X1~c(i1,i1)*1+c(ba,ba)*age+c(bs,bs)*sex1 #HERE, I REGRESS OUT THE EFFECT OF AGE

a1~~1*a1
a2~~1*a2
c1~~1*c1
c2~~1*c2
e1~~1*e1
e2~~1*e2
a1+a2+c1+c2+e1+e2~0*1 #fix means of latent factors to 0
'

messages.subject: Re: Latent Variable with Two Indicators
messages.subject_clean: Latent Variable with Two Indicators
messages.body_plain:
> I was wondering how I would go about specifying a latent variable with only two indicators.

There are a couple of ways to set the scale of the construct.  If you fix both factor loadings to 1, you can estimate both residual indicator variances, and the factor variance will be the observed covariance between the indicators.  If you fix the latent variance to 1, you can estimate the factor loadings, but the loadings would have to be constrained to equality if it were the only factor in the model.  If there are other factors in the model, you should be able to estimate both (unique) factor loadings, but it depends on whether the 2-indicator factor is exogenous/endogenous, and how it relates to other exogenous/endogenous factors in the model.

I found this article very enlightening:

dx.doi.org/10.1037//1082-989X.7.2.210 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1037//1082-989X.7.2.210>

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Almut,
If you would like to define the second-order variables, do it the same way as other first-order variables.

For example,
f1 =~ item1 + item2 + item3
f2 =~ item4 + item5 + item6 + item7
f3 =~ f1 + f2
In this example, the variables item1 to item7 are observed variables. Therefore, the latent variables f1 and f2 are ﬁrst-order factors. The latent variable f3 is a second-order factor,
since all of its indicators are latent variables themselves.
see:
http://users.ugent.be/~yrosseel/lavaan/lavaanJSSpreview.pdf
Page 6.
And don't forget specify the covariances if needed.

> why ML and MLM give different degree of freedom and the value of its minimum function test statistic also?can anyone explain me about it, please?
>

> >                                # Run bootstraping

The bootstrapLavaan() function does not return a "lavaan" object (i.e., the object with your all your model results, such as SEM.model above).  It simply returns the bootstrap distribution of whatever function you want to apply to a lavaan object.  Above, you apply the "coef" function (FUN = "coef"), so your object SEM.model.boot is simply the "distribution" (of size R = 10) of each coefficient in SEM.model

I think what you want to do is tell lavaan that you want bootstrapped SEs when you call sem(), then your call to parameterEstimates() will function as you expect.

> nBoots <- 1000
> SEM.model <- sem(Model, data = Dataset, se = "boot", test = "Bollen.Stine", bootstrap = nBoots)
> parameterEstimates(SEM.model, boot.ci.type = "norm", standardized = TRUE)
>

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Bootstrapping parameter estimate CIs
messages.subject_clean: Bootstrapping parameter estimate CIs
messages.body_plain:
On 05/26/2014 03:21 AM, Conal Monaghan wrote:
> Thanks Terry!
>
>                 I ran the code and the parameterEstimates() function
> worked (see below). This call has produced the parameter estimates with
> bootstrapped conventional standard errors. Now that this function is
> returning without errors, I was hoping to produce the CI's for the
> standardized parameter estimates (and later down the track several fit
> indices). As a result, bootstrapping the "coef" function should produce
> a distribution on these estimates from which the 95% CI could be
> determined through the parameterEstimates() function. I was wondering
> how I these estimates could be produced?

To bootstrap the standardized estimates, you need to use the
bootstrapLavaan() function again. As follows:

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)

out <- bootstrapLavaan(fit, R = 100, FUN = function(x) {
standardizedSolution(x)$est }, verbose = TRUE)

This will return a 100x24 matrix (in practice, you may want to use a
much larger number for R). The rows are the bootstraps, the columns are
the model parameters (here including fixed parameters).

To get a 95% CI, you can compute percentiles on the columns of out:

# just one column:
quantile(out[,1], probs=c(0.025, 0.975))

# all columns
lapply(as.data.frame(out), quantile, probs=c(0.025, 0.975))

To bootstrap one of more fit measures, you can use something like:

out <- bootstrapLavaan(fit, R = 100, FUN = function(x) { fitMeasures(x,
c("cfi", "rmsea")) }, verbose = TRUE)

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Adjust calculation of Satorra-Bentler scaling factor for multigroup analysis with varying items
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am running multigroup CFA in Lavaan and (because of nonnormality) want to adjust the model chisquare. However, I do not want to do that with the built-in Satorra-Bentler scaling factor, but with a version of the Satorra-Bentler scaling factor that would only based on parts of the matrices that typically go into its calculation. I wonder whether anyone could suggest a (relatively easy) way to do so in the R/Lavaan environment. Any help would be very much appreciated.

Below, I sketch the background of my request.

I am trying to follow the procedure suggested by Baumgartner and Steenkamp (1998) for multigroup analysis with varying numbers of observed variables in the different groups. Suppose observed variable A is not measured in the Group 1. Their "trick" then is to impute random values for the missing values that A has in Group 1, while making sure that A has zero mean, unit variance, and zero covariances with all other items, in which case the sample variances and covariances of A can be perfectly reproduced by the CFA/SEM model. As such, the imputation of values does not affect the model chisquare.

However, the imputation of values does lead to incorrect goodness of fit measures like CFI, TLI, RMSEA and SRMR, due to the fact that the degrees of freedom and the number of "observed" covariances are artificially increased. Still correct fit measures can easily be calculated from the Lavaan output. However, the imputed values also affect the Satorra-Bentler scaling factor and I am still looking for a (hopefully relatively easy) way to get the correct scaling factor.

I have attached some Lavaan output as an example (for simplicity in an analysis with one group only) for the problem I am facing. The file "nlgen.all1.mlm.txt" is from CFA without the observed variables Ethical20, Ethical32, and Ethical19 (and without their underlying factor Ethical), whereas the file "nlgen.all1.mlm.fill.normal.txt" is from CFA with the observed variables Ethical20, Ethical32, and Ethical19 which got imputed values. As you can see, the ML model chisquare stays the same, but CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR, and , worst of all, the Satorra-Bentler scaling factor changed.

Kind regards,
Ivo van der Lans

messages.body_plain:
(This question is from the same project as that which gave rise to my previous correspondence, but concerns a separate issue.)

I am fitting a parallel latent CTT model, in which all the factor loadings are constrained to be equal, using the cfa() function in lavaan.  When I test a case with only 4 items, the estimation matches that from Mplus Version 7.  When I fit a model with 5 items, the values of the loadings match Mplus in magnitude, but with opposite sign.  (I also observe this behavior with more items than 5.)  When I run the unconstrained (congeneric) case, cfa() estimates loadings that are similar to one another and the correct sign.  It is not clear to me how I have erroneously defined the model to give rise to this discrepancy.  I am hoping you can help.

I have included several files to document this behavior:
lavaan_poll_test_case.R is R code.  First I fit the 4-item congeneric model, then the 4-item parallel model, to demonstrate proper fit.  Then I fit the 5-item congeneric and parallel models to demonstrate the anomaly with the parallel fit.

pll_test_case_lavaan_compare_4item.out--output file from Mplus version 7 64-bit running on this same machine, in which I fit the 4-item model.

pll_test_case_lavaan_compare_5item.out--Mplus output file for the 5-item model.

Thank you for your assistance.

Sincerely,
Lisa Henn

messages.subject: Re: Anomalous Fit, Parallel Latent CTT Model using cfa()
messages.subject_clean: Anomalous Fit, Parallel Latent CTT Model using cfa()
messages.body_plain:
Lisa--
     Signs can be "reversed" (from what is expected) when the factor's variance is set directly--by fixing it to a value like 1, versus indirectly, by fixing a loading to a value like 1.  With the first approach, the Loadings are actually indeterminate with regard to sign.  You can see this in the formula for the variance of an observed variable Y that loads on a factor, F:

Variance(Y) = Loading squared times variance(F) + variance(error)

Since the loading is squared, both positive and negative signs produce the same covariance structure, hence the same fit.  This indeterminacy can extend across the whole covariance matrix of Y, making the signs of the Loadings arbitrary, as long as complementary signs are chosen for all observed variables.

     If this makes you uncomfortable, you can set starting values for Loadings with the sign you want, and that will lead to convergence with the desired signs on your loading estimates.  If you want positive Loadings, set a few positive starting values.  You will need a second pass through your model syntax--one to set the equality constraints that you want, and a second one to set starting values.

Programs differ in how they choose automatic starting values.  Some may impose positive starting values for Loadings as a default, while others may take a different approach.  Trust me, it is not the weirdest thing about factor models.

--Ed Rigdon

Sent from my iPad

Like Ed pointed out: there is nothing anomalous about this. The signs of
the factor loadings are arbitrary.

To give a 'hint' about the sign, you can use something like:

model <- '
      Skill =~ v1*item1 + v1*item2 + v1*item3 + v1*item4 + v1*item5 +
start(0.5)*item5
'

(note that I changed the starting value of the last item, since we use
this one when all of them are constrained to be equal).

fit <- cfa(model, data=test.data, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)
summary(fit)

gives you positive values again.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: naive bootstrap standard errors and Bollen and Stine boostrap chi-sq p-value
messages.subject_clean: naive bootstrap standard errors and Bollen and Stine boostrap chi-sq p-value
messages.body_plain:
The Bollen-Stine (or "model-based") bootstrap rescales the observed data so that they are consistent with the null hypothesis of perfect fit (i.e., it begins by transforming the data so that the observed means and covariance matrix are identical to the model-implied means and covariance matrix).  This is so that the bootstrapped distribution of chi-squared statistics (and by implication, the p-value/probability of a chi-sq at least as large as your observed chi-sq) is consistent with the null hypothesis.  You do not use Bollen-Stine method to calculate SEs or CIs for your parameters.

If you can't obtain the Bollen-Stine article because your library doesn't have access to Sociological Method and Research, perhaps they have access to Multivariate Behavioral Research.  A 2009 article (URL below) reviews this method and generalizes it for use with missing data.

dx.doi.org/10.1080/00273170903333590 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/00273170903333590>

Terry
